::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

- Read settings from a YAML file with `configfile:` and the `config` dictionary.
- Read a samplesheet with pandas and build sample names from its columns.
- Write an input function that looks up a sample's control.
- Group samples by a column (all replicates of one target) for a rule that
  combines them.
- Override config values from the command line, and know when not to.

Time: 45 min
:::

## What is still in the code

Stopping point A has two things that change from project to project written
into the Snakefile:

```{.python filename="stopping-points/stopA/Snakefile"}
SAMPLES = [
    "HCT116_CTCF_1", "HCT116_CTCF_2",
    ...
]
MIN_MAPQ = 30
```

A new project means editing the workflow, and nothing says which MAPQ a given
result used, except the code as it was that day. The lab pipelines keep both
outside: a **samplesheet** for the samples, a **config file** for the
settings. This module starts from stopping point A (copy it if you need to).

## A config file

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="config/RegConfig.yaml" lines="48-52" >}}

Point the Snakefile at it:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" lines="14-19" >}}

`configfile:` reads the YAML into a dictionary called `config` before any rule
is defined. `config["minMapq"]` is `30`, an integer, because YAML says so.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
For now, keep stopping point A's `filter` rule as it is and only change where
the numbers come from:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
MIN_MAPQ = config["minMapq"]
EXCLUDE_FLAGS = config["excludeFlags"]
```

Module 4 moves them into the rule's `params:`, for a reason you will see there.
The paths `../../data` and `output` become config keys too (`dataDir`,
`outputDir`), so the pipeline can run from anywhere.
:::

## The samplesheet

One row per sequencing library, tab-separated. The columns are the same as in
the lab's other pipelines:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="RegSamplesheet.txt" lang="text" >}}

`Control` holds the *name* of the control sample, or `NA`. The config says
where the sheet is and which columns make a name:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="config/RegConfig.yaml" lines="9-13" >}}

## Reading it with pandas

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" lines="27-37" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- `dtype=str` keeps every column as text. Without it, `Bio_Rep` is read as the
  integer `1`, and `"_".join` stops with
  `TypeError: sequence item 2: expected str instance, int found`.
- Line 33 joins the `fileNamesFrom` columns: `HCT116`, `CTCF`, `1` become
  `HCT116_CTCF_1`. Change the config to `['Target', 'Bio_Rep']` and every
  name, and every output path, changes with it.
- `SAMPLE_TABLE` is the same table indexed by sample name, so
  `SAMPLE_TABLE.loc["HCT116_CTCF_1", "Control"]` is one lookup.
- `SAMPLES` is the list `rule all` used to have typed in.
:::

## The `NA` trap

`keep_default_na=False` on line 30 matters. By default pandas turns the text
`NA` into a missing value (`NaN`), so the test `control == "NA"` is false for
DNase, and the pipeline looks for a control called `nan`:

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-no-keep-na | stopping-points/stopB | sed -i 's/, keep_default_na=False//' Snakefile && snakemake -n 2>&1 | grep -v 'strict channel priorities' || true -->

{{< generated name="stopB-no-keep-na" command="false" >}}

`output/nan/nan_filtered.bam` is the clue. When a path contains `nan`, look at
how the table was read.

::: {.notes}
This one cost a real afternoon while the course pipeline was being written.
It is worth the slide.
:::

## Inputs that come from a lookup

So far every input was a pattern: fill in `{sample}`, get a path. The FASTQ
path now comes from the samplesheet (`Sequencing_Directory` plus `Read1`),
which need not look like the sample name at all. For that, `input:` takes a
**function**:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" def="fastq" >}}

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule fastqc:
    input:
        fastq = fastq,          # the function itself, not fastq()
```

Snakemake calls the function once per job with that job's `wildcards` and
uses whatever path it returns. You pass the function, without parentheses.

## The control lookup

Peak calling needs each ChIP sample's control, and DNase has none:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" def="control_bam" >}}

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" lines="220-227" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
For `HCT116_CTCF_1` the function returns
`output/HCT116_input-CTCF_1/HCT116_input-CTCF_1_filtered.bam`, so the peak
job waits for that control to be filtered too. For `HCT116_DNase_1` it
returns an empty list, which means "no input here", and the job runs with the
treatment BAM only.

`treatment` is a `lambda`, a one-line function written in place. It does the
same as a `def` and is handy when the body is a single expression.
`filtered_bam()` is a small helper (lines 59-60) so the path is spelled once,
in one place, and `rule all` and the rules cannot drift apart.
:::

## Which samples get peaks

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" lines="39-45" >}}

A sample is a control if another row names it. Every other sample (the four
ChIP samples and the two DNase samples) gets peaks. `TARGETS` is
`['CTCF', 'H3K27ac', 'DNase']`, and `SAMPLES_BY_TARGET` maps each target to
its replicates.

## One job per target

Consensus peaks combine the replicates of one target, so the wildcard is
`{target}`, and the input function returns a different number of files per
target:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" lines="252-257" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The output has `{target}`, so `rule all` asks for
`output/consensus/CTCF_consensus.bed` and Snakemake sets `target=CTCF`. The
input function uses that to fetch the peak files of `HCT116_CTCF_1` (as
`first`) and `HCT116_CTCF_2` (in `others`). A third CTCF replicate in the
samplesheet would join `others`, with no change to the rule.
:::

## Lists of files with `expand()` in an input function

MicroCPipe does the same kind of grouping with `expand()`. Its `dedup` rule
merges every sequencing run of one library:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" rule="dedup" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`expand()` fills in `{run}` from the list for this group. `{{group}}` is an
escaped brace: `expand()` leaves it as a literal `{group}` instead of
complaining that you gave it no `group` list. Snakemake then fills that
`{group}` from the job's own wildcards. The [field guide](../field-guide/microcpipe.qmd#mc-input-functions)
walks through it line by line.
:::

## Keep wildcards to real names

With names now coming from the samplesheet, stopping point B restricts the
wildcards to them, the same way MicroCPipe does (module 2):

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" lines="47-51" >}}

Without them, `{sample}` in `output/peaks/{sample}_peaks.narrowPeak` would
match any text at all. With them it can only be a name from the samplesheet,
and a typo in a target fails at once with "No rule to produce".

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
At this point, with `call_peaks` and `consensus_peaks` added to your
Snakefile and to `rule all`, a dry run plans 41 jobs: the 31 from stopping
point A, 6 `call_peaks`, 3 `consensus_peaks` and `all`. Module 4 adds the
bigWigs and brings it to stopping point B.
:::

## Changing a setting for one run

`--config` sets a value on the command line, on top of the config file:

```bash
snakemake -n --config minMapq=20
```

That works for a top-level number. For anything nested, it does not do what
you expect. This tiny Snakefile prints `config["window"]`:

```bash
printf 'configfile: "config/RegConfig.yaml"\nprint(config["window"])\n' > show.smk
snakemake -s show.smk -n --config 'window={"start": 128000000}'
```

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-config-string | stopping-points/stopB | printf 'configfile: "config/RegConfig.yaml"\nprint(config["window"])\n' > show.smk && snakemake -s show.smk -n --config 'window={"start": 128000000}' -->

{{< generated name="stopB-config-string" command="false" >}}

The other keys survive, but `start` is now the **string** `'128000000'`. Values
inside a `--config` dictionary all arrive as text, so `{"enabled": false}`
arrives as `'false'`, and a non-empty string counts as true in Python. The
course pipeline's `ttseq: enabled: false` cannot be switched off this way.

## Use `--configfile` for anything nested

Put the change in a small YAML file instead:

```{.yaml filename="narrow.yaml"}
window:
  start: 128000000
```

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-configfile-int | stopping-points/stopB | printf 'configfile: "config/RegConfig.yaml"\nprint(config["window"])\n' > show.smk && printf 'window:\n  start: 128000000\n' > narrow.yaml && snakemake -s show.smk -n --configfile narrow.yaml -->

```bash
snakemake -s show.smk -n --configfile narrow.yaml
```

{{< generated name="stopB-configfile-int" command="false" >}}

The file named in `configfile:` is read first, then yours on top, key by key.
Types are YAML's, so the number is a number.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `--config` and `--configfile` take more than one value

Both options swallow every word after them, so a target written last is read
as another config entry (or another file) and the run fails before it starts.
Put targets first, or end the list with `--`:

```bash
snakemake -n output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak --config minMapq=20
snakemake -n --config minMapq=20 -- output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak
```
:::

A labmate renamed the `Bio_Rep` column of the samplesheet to `Rep`, because

```bash
sed -i '1s/Bio_Rep/Rep/' RegSamplesheet.txt
snakemake -n
```

## Key points

- `configfile:` loads YAML into `config`. Paths, thresholds and switches live
  there, not in the rules.
- Read the samplesheet with `dtype=str, keep_default_na=False`; build sample
  names from the columns listed in `fileNamesFrom`.
- An input function receives `wildcards` and returns the job's inputs. Use it
  for lookups (the control) and for groups (the replicates of a target).
  Returning `[]` means "no input".
- `{{name}}` inside `expand()` leaves a wildcard for Snakemake to fill later.
- `--config key=value` is fine for top-level values. For nested keys, use a
  small YAML file with `--configfile`.
